newsitem.title: USA: U.S. study questions programs for premature babies.
newsitem.headline: U.S. study questions programs for premature babies.

text.p: A study published on Tuesday cast doubt on the long-term effectiveness of special programmes in the first few years of life to help premature babies overcome developmental and intellectual problems.

The study involved more than 870 children who weighed less than 5.5 pounds (2.5 kg) at birth, 336 of whom were given special treatment up to age 3 including home visits, sessions at child development centres and parental group meetings.
At 3 years, there were striking differences between the children given special treatment and those who were not, the report from Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York said.

But by age 8, overall intelligence test scores, cognitive skills, school achievement, behaviour and health were similar in both groups, said the report, published in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association.

"Our findings suggest that programmatic efforts need to distinguish between heavier and lighter low-birthweight infants. The programme did help children with birth weights of 4.4 lbs (2 kg) or less at age 3 years but clearly these effects were smaller and not sustained," the study said.

Researchers said children who were heaviest at birth had a four-point edge on IQ scores at the age of 8, compared to those who weighed less. "At the same time it is reasonable to question the economic price involved in sustaining a four-point IQ difference ... the cost of delivering the (treatment programs) was estimated at $15,146 per child," they said.

The report added that there may be a need for different or continued support for low birthweight infants beyond age 3. "The corresponding low mean IQ scores and high rates of school failure of low birthweight children underscore the importance of public health efforts to reduce premature births," it said.
